Title: Service successes boost foreign trade
text: PRESS CONFERENCE 20. MAY 2014 Service successes boost foreign trade Current developments in the Austrian balance of payments Likes. Andreas Ittner Deputy Governor Likes. Dr. Johannes Turner Director of the Department of Statistics Page 1 Summary of key developments in 2013  Austria is once again generating solid current account growth. At EUR 8.5 billion or 2.7% of GDP, the surplus once again significantly exceeded the good result of 2012 (EUR 7.3 billion). Austria has so far coped comparatively well with the challenges of the globally unfavourable economic environment and continues to be one of the competitive and macro-economically stable countries.  The chemistry between Austria and its trading partners is right. Between 2007 and 2013, chemical products made the main contribution to growth in domestic exports. Food and beverages as well as machinery and vehicles follow at a considerable distance.13% of exports are in the field of cutting-edge technology.  Austria's service providers are sailing on a record course. At EUR 15.4 billion, the services balance shows a historic record surplus. A high proportion of technology and innovation, which mainly comes from IT, architecture and engineering services, testifies to an increasingly modern orientation of the service sector. The importance of transport, on the other hand, is declining.  Tourism industry celebrates the most successful year in its history. Foreign tourists spent more than EUR 15 billion in Austria in 2013, more than ever before. In view of a slight decline in Austrians' expenditure on outbound travel, the surplus from the travel balance rose to EUR 7.5 billion, also an unprecedented figure.  However, all these successes are not a cushion of peace! Constant efforts are needed to maintain the competitiveness and location quality of the internationally strongly networked domestic economy.  Securities business with foreign countries continues to suffer from crisis paralysis. Austria's international investment as well as the financing by means of securities is not gaining momentum. The bond business is stagnating. At best, private households are showing certain signs of a revival in view of the renewed interest in investment funds.  Eastern Europe, please wait! Austria's direct investment in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe collapsed in 2013. The investment volume of EUR 1.5 billion was the lowest since 1999. Only Croatia, the Czech Republic and the Republic of Serbia were able to place among the top ten. In the long term, however, this region will remain interesting for domestic companies. In 2013, more than 80% of investments went to the Netherlands, Germany and Norway. The trade deficit has halved: EUR -3.8 billion. Trade in goods could not escape the weak global growth. Exports have developed weakly and imports have declined. The surplus from trade in services reached the highest level ever recorded: EUR 15.4 billion. Both tourism and other commercial service providers - in particular engineering, IT and trade - have now overtaken the previous highs recorded in 2008, before the financial and fiscal crisis. Even if the balance of income streams in the year under review shows a small minus, a positive trend is unmistakable. The persistent surpluses in trade in services continuously reduce foreign debt, which automatically relieves the income balance. The surpluses that have been recorded for around ten years have helped to reduce the foreign debt that had previously been built up. The economy of the euro area as a whole emerged from recession in 2013 and is expected to pick up speed in the course of the current year (EU Commission forecast: 1.2%). The external imbalances of the Member States, which had large current account deficits, are gradually improving. The accumulated external debt, on the other hand, is decreasing only slowly. The recovery is therefore still fragile and export development requires the support of growth sectors, especially the service sector. Little attention is paid to the major role that foreign corporations play in Austria for foreign trade: 45% of the exports of goods manufacturers and 42% of the exports of services (excluding travel) are accounted for by foreign-controlled companies. Their share is particularly high (more than 50%) in the automotive industry and pharmaceuticals as well as in the innovative areas of research and development as well as computer and information services. Securing the attractiveness of the location is therefore of essential importance for the further development of Austria's current account. Austria's goods export "goes global" In 2013, growth impulses for domestic goods exports came from Russia and the oil-exporting countries of the Middle East. Since the outbreak of the financial crisis, target markets outside the EU have become increasingly important for Austrian industry as a whole. They now account for a third of goods exports. Sales to the BRICS countries1 grew by 9% p.a., to the future markets "Next 11"2 by 5% p.a. and amounted to a total of EUR 13 billion of total export revenues in 2013. The Russian Federation is now one of the ten most important target markets and China is already ranked 11th. Growth impulses from the EU in 2013 came mainly from France and the United Kingdom (both 5%). The first signs of an upturn in exports were seen in Hungary (7%), Poland (5%) and Slovenia (8%). During the financial crisis, the pharmaceutical industry supported the export trend In 2013, machinery and vehicles, which traditionally form the most important export sector in Austria, recorded the highest growth (4.3% or 2 to EUR 49 billion). However, over the entire period from 2007 to 2013, which was marked by the financial and fiscal crisis, the highest contribution to growth came from the chemical pharmaceutical industry, which proved its resistance to crises. In 2013, their export volume amounted to EUR 16.6 billion, which corresponds to 13.4% of total exports of goods, placing them in third place behind machinery and vehicles as well as semi-finished goods. The export value of all manufactured goods from Austria amounted to EUR 80.2 billion. This corresponds to around two-thirds of total exports. Only 22% was accounted for by semi-finished goods, which are used in the production of consumer or capital goods in other countries. The Austrian export structure thus allows a high proportion of global added value generated in the course of production at locations in several countries to be generated domestically. However, it should not be forgotten that domestic suppliers are among the market leaders worldwide, for example in the paper and goods made of mineral materials (building materials, insulation materials, refractory goods). In order to assert itself against competitors worldwide, no longer individual goods, but system packages are exported and the delivery of goods is enriched with accompanying advice, training, advertising, assembly and repair. In addition to unit prices and the duration of trade settlement, product differentiation is one of the most important competitive factors in goods trading, especially in the technology sectors. Accordingly, the mechanical engineering, automotive and electronics sectors in Austria are among the most important service exporters. In addition to engineering and other technical services, research and development services are provided abroad. In these types of services, industry has an export share of more than 50% and thus a higher priority than the corresponding service sectors. While modern information technologies facilitate global market access (e.g. through software downloads or online training), most services are still based on personal interaction between provider and customer, which limits their reach. The neighbouring countries and the member states of the EU are therefore the most important target market for the export of services from Austria. A shift in trade in trade in goods in favour of third countries, as can be observed in trade in goods, does not take place in trade in services. On the contrary, the importance of Germany as the most important sales market increased further in 2013: 6% or EUR 0.7 billion to EUR 12.2 billion. Chart 5 in billion EUR 40 35 30 25 20 15 10 5 0 2013 The IT industry drives Austria's exports In contrast to trade in goods, whose growth almost came to a standstill under the sovereign debt crisis in the euro area and the subdued economy in developing and emerging countries, services remained largely unimpressed: exports expanded by 9% in 2012 and by 5% in 2013. This is mainly due to services with a high proportion of innovation and technology. These include IT service providers who develop customer-specific software and offer hardware and network support, but also the offer of architects and engineers. Technical services accounted for 28% of total export revenues in 2013, or EUR 9.4 billion in absolute terms. In the long term, the share increased by 15 percentage points. The importance of the most important export category, transport, has decreased in the course of the financial, fiscal and economic crisis and is stagnating in the long term. In addition to a high degree of dependence on economic developments, domestic providers are confronted with competition from low-cost providers from Eastern Europe. The importance of other, traditional types of services such as construction and trade is also declining in the long term. These are the highest revenues ever generated. In view of a slight decline in Austrians' expenditure on outbound travel, the surplus from the travel balance rose to EUR 7.5 billion, also an unprecedented figure. With almost 25 million arrivals of foreigners, a record result was achieved for the fourth time in uninterrupted order. Statistics Austria also recorded a clear increase in overnight stays for foreigners in the 2013 reporting year with 96.8 million overnight stays (1.9%). Only in 1991 and 1992, in the wake of German reunification, had this figure been exceeded. Including domestic guests, 2013 also recorded a historic maximum of 132.6 million overnight stays. In 2012, the IMF ranks Austria 13th in terms of tourism revenues: only the USA, China and the major European destinations, as well as Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Australia are ahead of Austria. Countries such as India, Canada, Japan or Switzerland have lower tourism revenues than Austria. The recipe for success: retaining regular guests and opening up new markets Two-thirds of the increase in overnight stays in 2013 was attributable to German guests (1.2 million overnight stays). Contrary to the long-term trend, their share increased in the year under review. There were declining overnight stays not only among guests from the crisis-ridden countries of the Mediterranean (Italy, Spain, Cyprus, Greece), but also among guests from France, the Netherlands or Ireland. The double-digit growth in the number of overnight stays by guests from Central and South-Eastern Europe over a long period of time has slowed noticeably (Slovenia 7.7%, Slovakia 6.0%, Czech Republic 1.2%, Poland 1.1%) and has occasionally also turned in the opposite direction (Hungary -0.2%, Romania -3.4%, Croatia -6.0%). Emerging economies show the strongest momentum: the World Tourism Organization reports that travel spending by Chinese and Russians has increased by 25-30% within a year. The Austrian overnight stay statistics recorded the strongest relative increases among guests from Korea (30%), the Arab world (20%), China (14%), as well as Russia, CIS and Ukraine (10%). Meanwhile, the number of overnight stays of Chinese guests (580,000) exceeds that of guests from Japan. Russia was the eighth most important country of origin in 2013 with almost 2 million overnight stays (well ahead of the USA and France). Themost important change concerns income from direct investment, where Austria has become a net investor since the opening up to the East and accession to the EU and has been generating net income on an ongoing basis since 2006. The fact that the income balance for 2013 nevertheless closes with a minus is the result of a "cautious" earnings estimate for direct investment. The declining surpluses in earned income are no cause for concern: the comparatively good employment situation in Austria leads to a growing attractiveness of Austria for cross-border commuters and seasonal workers. In 2013, there were positive transactions of EUR 1.8 billion for domestic funds and EUR 1.2 billion for foreign funds. Since 2011, there has been a clear upward trend in the purchase of certificates. Domestic funds were sold to a high degree by the Austrian household sectorduring the crisis, while foreign funds continued to be bought, albeit only slightly. In particular, those funds that invest in short- and long-term interest-bearing securities were removed from household portfolios. Domestic funds are comparatively important for Austrian investors and therefore benefit disproportionately from the current upward trend. Overall, the portfolio of foreign funds - especially equity funds - rose by 16% year-on-year to just under EUR 10 billion at the end of 2013. Active and passive direct investment flows (excluding real estate and special purpose vehicles) wereat an average level of EUR 101/2 billion and EUR 81/2 billion respectively in 2013. This is all the more true when one takes into account that it includes a transaction of EUR 3 billion via a regional 'bridgehead'. However, Austrian investments in Central, Eastern and South-Eastern Europe fell significantly in 2013. The investment volume of EUR 1.5 billion was the lowest since 1999. Only Croatia, the Czech Republic and the Republic of Serbia were able to place among the top ten. More than 80% of investments in 2013 went to the Netherlands, Germany and Norway. The withdrawal of the Verbundgesellschaft from Turkey, which has exchanged its still young investments in Turkey for power plants in Germany, made a significant contribution to this result. The record investments in Norway are due to OMV's increased efforts to extract crude oil in the North Sea. In addition to energy suppliers, banks, insurance companies and real estate investors as well as mechanical engineering companies invested abroad in 2013. Passive direct investment in 2013 came mainly from Russia, Germany, Luxembourg and Hungary. From an industry perspective, the telecommunications sector, the automotive sector, mechanical engineering, banks and trading companies stand out. Income from foreign owners also reached historic highs of EUR 9.3 billion. Although dividend payments in 2013 were about 10% lower than in 2012, 2013 should also bring good returns for most investors. The OeNB anticipates declining active and rising passive income. Looking at a 10-year period, Austria's active direct investment generated EUR 961/2 billion in profits. The subsidiaries were particularly successful in the Czech Republic, followed by Germany, Switzerland, China and Russia. Page 17 September makes everything new The global economy is subject to constant change. Therefore, it is necessary to adjust the statistics from time to time. In 2009, in addition to the new system of national accounts, the IMF also adopted new rules on the compilation of the balance of payments and the international asset position. After the USA, Canada and Australia have already changed their statistics, European economic statistics will now also be put on this new basis in September this year. The new statistics will provide more detail in strategically important areas such as research and development. It contains more detailed rules on the treatment of "contract processing", which is becoming increasingly important in the course of the progressive global division of labour. Statistical systems are better coordinated (GDP generation, use, distribution, financing, external accounts, balance sheet, changes in assets) and comparability between different countries should also improve. The OeNB does not expect any dramatic changes in the Austrian current account, but shifts within the performance area will result in noticeable changes in individual subheadings. In order to be able to continue to analyse changes over time, the OeNB will offer a complete retrospective calculation for the years from 2006 onwards. Particularly important aggregates are to be recalculated by 1995. Finally, the OeNB would like to thank all the reporters who contribute to the preparation of the balance of payments  in addition to banks and insurance companies about 5,000 large and small companies but also thousands of households  for their cooperation. Das Handelsdefizit hat sich halbiert: -3,8 Mrd EUR. Der Gterhandel konnte sich der weltweiten Wachstumsschwche nicht entziehen. Die Exporte entwickelten sich schwach, die Importe sind zurckgegangen.  Der berschuss aus dem Dienstleistungsverkehr erreichte den hchsten bislang gemessenen Wert: 15,4 Mrd EUR.  Sowohl der Tourismus als auch die brigen kommerziellen Dienstleister - vor allem das Ingenieurswesen, die EDV-Branche und der Handel - haben die bisherigen Hchstwerte, die im Jahr 2008 und damit vor der Finanz- und Fiskalkrise verzeichnet wurden, inzwischen berholt. Title: The Digitalization Challenge: Some Remarks From the Perspective of a Central Bank as Technology User
text: Peter Mooslechner Executive Director Oesterreichische Nationalbank SPEECH Check against delivery! Vienna, June 26, 2018 The Digitalization Challenge: Some Remarks from the Perspective of a Central Bank as Technology User1 Keynote at the 5th Central Bank Executive Summit Good morning, everybody! Ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues! It's a great pleasure for me to welcome you all here in Vienna at the premises of Oesterreichische Nationalbank on the occasion of this outstanding event, the 5th Annual Central Bank Executive Summit. I hope you all had a smooth journey to Vienna, enjoyed yesterday evening, and  looking at the program  there is more to come in the course of the next three days. I am very happy to see so many colleagues from the central banking world and I hope you will find some time to take in the city of Vienna  and to spend some money here. By way of introduction, let me  at the very beginning of this summit  touch very briefly on some elements that will shape our central banking world over the forthcoming decade, or that will be of relevance for the fulfillment of our tasks at least. It seems that these developments happen rather quickly nowadays, perhaps much more quickly than the usual frequency of change at central banks, and even if it is neither our habit nor wise to jump on any bandwagon, to embrace any new development immediately, we at least have to understand, (i) first, what is going on and (ii) second, how relevant these developments will be for our own work. In economics there is this well-known model of the conservative central banker! Fortunately, it does not deal with individual habits and preferences of central bankers, but it is about the reaction function of central banks as policymakers and it reflects the expectation of the general public, who 1 Many thanks to Beat Weber for excellent substantive input to this text. Publisher and editor: Oesterreichische Nationalbank Communications Division Editor in chief: Christian Gutlederer Otto-Wagner-Platz 3, 1010 Vienna, PO Box 61 has entrusted us with the task of maintaining the stability of money and finance via prudent policies. With regard to technology, the implications are less clear. What I see is that most of my colleagues are very experienced in all kinds of mobile and digital communication today. Most central banks also try to stay up-to-date with the latest technological developments that serve their interests as institutional users. But being conservative as a central bank certainly also means being skeptical whenever narrow views  or too enthusiastic views - of technological progress conflict with or ignore common sense. I presume it is our joint expertise in economics, finance, banking and many other areas that makes central banks comparatively difficult customers for consultants and suppliers eager to sell the latest technological advances. But being skeptical does certainly not mean being unreasonable with regard to using new technology. Digitalization comes as an opportunity as well as a challenge to central banks, depending on its specific field of application and its particular use. Although I am definitely not an expert in technology, let me mention a number of likely or relevant effects of digitalization in several fields of central bank activity. We are all aware that the central banking world has changed significantly in the course of the crisis and in reaction to the crisis. In a similar way, central banks have to deal with the revolution caused by digitalization. It creates a need for change in  potentially many areas and the management of central banks has to identify the relevant broader perspective of making this change beneficial, successful and meaningful. Let me very quickly touch upon five selected aspects of digitalization here: 1. Digitalization can be expected to bring the benefit of increased efficiency to existing areas Digitalization is generally expected to increase efficiency and to reduce costs. This can be the case, for example, in regulation and supervision (RegTech, SupTech) as well as in the integration of market infrastructure systems. Digital tools may help us to automate and streamline administrative and operational procedures, digitize data and working tools, and improve data analytics. We might one day be technically able to monitor a financial institutions positions or transactions or client reports live and off-site to prevent noncompliance, or streamline data collection by automating the reporting process of financial institutions. In the end, there may be fewer on-site audits necessary, and reporting may take less time.2 A number of examples for what this may look like will be presented in the course of the conference. 2. Digitalization may help address shifting user demands Digitalization and the growth of online commerce results in increased user demand for payments in digital form, on mobile devices and at greater speed  in real time. 2 Seite 2 von 5 In reaction, central banks are induced to adapt their infrastructure, i.e. settlement services, to cope with these needs, in line with the services of commercial banks and other private entities for their customers. Under special circumstances, some central banks even think about providing greater direct access for retail customers to their payment services beyond cash. In the Eurosystem, TIPS is a major project in that respect, providing instant settlement in central bank money for instant payment solutions provided by private payment service providers. Some central banks, for example Sveriges Riksbank, go even further, and also investigate the possible issuance of digital base money to its population. Obviously, such a step would have huge potential social implications that go far beyond technological aspects: they concern the role of central banks in society, the division of labor within the financial sector and the balancing of privacy in financial affairs. In this country, it is the conservative attitude and a strong preference for cash of retail customers rather than the conservative attitude of central bankers that makes us feel there is currently no need for any revolutionary change to the existing mix of means of payment (beyond the ongoing adaptions to the payment service infrastructure that are underway). 3. Digitalization may facilitate information management or rather: the production of analytical knowledge - in some areas Big data analysis is another important aspect of a digitalized world to be mentioned here. Without going into detail, I would like to point out that it may enrich our statistical analyses and our knowledge about private sector activity relevant to central bank policies. The development of credit registers is an example, if not a key focus, of many central banks big data projects, closely followed by administrative sources and the consolidation of internal systems. But, in principle, big data has its potential in almost all fields of central bank activities. 4. Digitalization may create substantial challenges in some areas Since the decline of barter trade as the dominant model of exchange, money  first privately organized, nowadays provided and guaranteed by the central bank  has become the most convenient form of payment. This basis of our financial system was not challenged for a very long time, despite the rise of new forms of non-cash payments, but seen as an increase in efficiency, and our market economies have developed well on the basis of this model. Does the  broadly debated  emergence of private cryptocurrencies significantly change this historical picture? At the moment, they certainly do not challenge the role of existing means of payment in everyday life. But they exist, they are used, and even if they are assets and not currencies, they may be used in payments to foster the circumvention of regulation and control, to pay for illegal goods in online markets, to launder money, to raise capital without investor protection, and ultimately, they create a new kind of financial risk. From a more general perspective, what seems much more important in terms of changing our traditional financial landscape based on new technologies is the rise of FinTechs. FinTechs are new competitors for banks in their traditional markets  at least in some of them  and the technology they introduce may contribute to increased efficiency and product development in the financial sector. But by restructuring the financial landscape, they also create a challenge not only to bank profitability but also to regulation and supervision. Seite 3 von 5 5. Digitalization is facilitating the creation and dispersion of myths, misleading ideas and misconceptions about money and banking  including what central banks do, what they intend to do and what they should do So far, the four selected aspects addressed obviously create new challenges and force traditional market participants  as well as institutions like central banks  to adapt to this new financial world and to deal with the changes it incorporates. At the same time, there are potential benefits of these new technologies and one can expect  or at least hope  that they will increase market efficiency and be beneficial overall. But there is another side of this coin, which looks much less beneficial and demands very careful analysis and cautious treatment. Lets look at this dark side just to complete the picture and to conclude: Modern economic systems rely on the division of labor, organized by private corporations competing in markets. Money is the main bond that holds this generally fragmented, decentralized system together. A crisis  like the one observed in 2008/2009  reminds everyone that unexpected and unlikely events with a large economic impact can happen from time to time. It reveals that the system depends on the behavior of a huge number of economic agents, in an arrangement that rests on a fragile process of market coordination. Because money is so essential to the functioning of our economic system, it has attracted all kinds of anxieties in history. Some people even see the existence of (fiat) money as the root cause of all crises. In fact, the basic problem might be that everybody is a user of money and able to use money (and knows that it is helpful to possess money), but hardly anybody understands what the monetary system is and how it works. Blockchain, the technological innovation behind Bitcoin and similar undertakings, has made it possible to create and transfer digital tokens privately, based on a private algorithm and in a decentralized way (and some people call this money), without the need for and the existence of a central institution. But these systems transport very misleading views on money at the same time. The media hype of recent years around so-called cryptocurrencies has been almost exclusively driven by their use as a speculative asset. The term currency comes as a complete misnomer in this regard, not least because the inherent instability of the value of these tokens makes them unattractive as a means of payment and unit of account. Nevertheless their spread and the discourse around them has served to spread and reinforce the idea that ideal money should consist of an indestructible substance of limited quantity, like in primitive commodity money systems. Such a view is in stark contrast to the institutional realities behind our current monetary system. Here, the key to the stable domestic purchasing power of money is the fact that it is the liability of an issuer that holds assets, managing the resulting balance sheet in order to stabilize the value of money. This contrast serves as an important reminder that the most advanced technology can sometimes be based on the most backward worldview, like commodity money; and that an innovative technology can create challenges that are largely social in character. Seite 4 von 5 While many industries, including the financial sector, are currently investigating the possibility of employing blockchain and various other technical innovations for various cost-saving purposes, there is no reason to expect that blockchain will, in general, eliminate the function of intermediaries like banks. To a large extent, financial intermediation and processing payments consists of taking over risks on behalf of customers, not simply of transferring invariant objects between persons (e.g. between payer and payee, saver and debtor etc.). Blockchain might provide a secure, decentralized way for transferring and recording digital tokens, but it neither eliminates nor absorbs risks regarding the tokens accessibility, value and liquidity. Unless these risks are borne by an intermediary, they remain with the individual customer. To conclude with: These examples I have touched upon show that technologies may be able to do a lot of things  many with beneficial effects, some with unfavorable consequences. Central banks certainly have to be aware of technological developments concerning their tasks and working processes. But they have to be very careful regarding the consequences of implementing innovations  in their own field as well as in financial markets. This particularly concerns innovations which might bear a stability risk potential for fundamental institutions in our society like money and banking. I hope it is with events like this conference that we all can contribute to a deepened understanding of what new technologies may offer on the one hand, but also  on the other hand  to the economic and social context in which technology, whether new or old, has to fulfill its function  hopefully in the hands of people who know what they are doing. Im looking forward to a stimulating conference, thank you very much for your attention! Seite 5 von 5

Title: 200 years of stock trading on the Deutsche Brse in Frankfurt
text: Univ.-Prof. Mag. Dr. Robert Holzmann Governor Oesterreichische Nationalbank NETWORK Frankfurt am Main, 09 September 2020 200 years of stock trading on the Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt Dear Sir or Madam, First of all, on behalf of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, I would like to extend my warmest congratulations on your anniversary "200 years of stock trading on the Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt". First mentioned in a document in 1606 as "burs", deutsche Borse in Frankfurt has developed into an indispensable globally important location for international securities trading in its more than 400-year history. Regardless of derivatives and financial products of any kind, two main categories of securities are traded on the world's stock exchanges: bonds and shares. Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt is no exception. For this reason, I would like to single out two crucial dates in their centuries-long success story, as both also have a connection to Austria, Vienna and, above all, to trading in bonds and equities. In 1778, the era of government bonds began in Frankfurt: Bethmann Bank placed the first million-euro bond for Joseph II; Kaiser in Vienna. When this first bond is placed in Frankfurt, a young composer plays the piano in the Palatinate town of Kirchheimbolanden less than 80km from here. His name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. He is 22 years old at the time and is already the role model of another composer whose name is linked to the history of stock trading in Frankfurt: Ludwig van Beethoven, then 8 years old. 42 years later, in 1820, stock trading finally followed bond trading in Frankfurt. The first share to be traded in Frankfurt is shares in the Austrian National Bank  founded as the Imperial and Royal Privileged Austrian National Bank. One of the first shareholders was Ludwig van Beethoven, 50 years old at the time. It isawarding a package of nine units at the current equivalent of around EUR 80,000. Beethoven opts for a "buy and hold" strategy that is quite successful from today's point of view and bequeaths the shares to his nephew Karl with a corresponding increase in value. Publisher and editor: Oesterreichische Nationalbank Press Office Vienna 9., Otto-Wagner-Platz 3 P.O. Box 61, 1010 Vienna Ladies and gentlemen, not only Beethoven's share purchase in Frankfurt is a success story, but also, and of course, the development of Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt itself. In the following decades, milestones such as the introduction of the DAX, the conversion to the XETRA trading system and finally the IPO of Deutsche Borse itself followed. I would therefore like to congratulate you once again on your anniversary and present you with an original facsimile of the so-called Beethoven share with the best wishes of the OeNB. This marked the beginning of the success story of stock trading in Frankfurt. So I allow myself to ring in today's trading day with the opening bell  may it be just as successful as the impressive history of Deutsche Borse in Frankfurt so far. Page 2 of 2

Title: Economic and legal issues of banking supervision: What happens next after the case of Commerzialbank Mattersburg
text: Univ.-Prof. Mag. Dr. Robert Holzmann Governor Oesterreichische Nationalbank NETWORK The spoken word applies Vienna, 21 October 2020 Economic and legal issues of banking supervision: What happens next after the case of Commerzialbank Mattersburg Speech at the Annual General Meeting of the Austrian Bank Scientific Society (BWG)1 Dear Sir or Madam, I am extremely pleased to be able to address you today at the Annual General Meeting of the Austrian Banking Society. I would like to take this opportunity to dedicate myself in my lecture to a current  presumed, that requires the legal system  criminal case. I believe that Commerzialbank Mattersburg offers enough aspects to hold several full-length events. Don't worry, I don't intend to start a lecture series with you here; nevertheless, I would like to take this opportunity to point out some very important aspects of this case and existing opportunities for improvement from my economic perspective. You, dear professional audience, are then hopefully the fertile ground on which my thoughts can sprout and continue to thrive. After my presentation, I will explain to you how the OeNB's Jubilee Fund can support legal and economic work on the subject. I would like to start with an aspect that, in my opinion, is not mentioned in the media discussion, but is of essential importance for the correct classification of the incidents that have become known  with the economic basis and justification for the establishment of banking supervision. After all, what is the central purpose of banking supervision? Well, essentially, it ensures compliance with regulatory standards laid down by the  in our case largely European  legislators and based on the recommendations of the Basel Banking Committee. Of course, these regulatory norms do not have an end in themselves, but of course try to achieve certain goals. And although some of these norms also have a certain creditor protection character inherent in them, they primarily pursue the 1 The lecture benefited from the valuable input of Michael Kaden, Peter Strobl, Anna Theresa Mayer and Armin Bahensky (all OeNB). Thank you very much. However, all responsibility for the content lies with me. Publisher and editor: Oesterreichische Nationalbank Press Office Vienna 9., Otto-Wagner-Platz 3 P.O. Box 61, 1010 Vienna The aim is to strengthen the stability of the entire banking and financial system. An economy would be inconceivable without a functioning banking system! However, the banking system is protected as an abstracted whole, but by no means a specific individual bank. Market exits of individual market participants are therefore not excluded, as evidenced by the fact that the Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive2 (BRRD) has created a complete set of rules for the resolution of banks in distress. Prior to the implementation of the BRRD, the lack of rules and instruments to safeguard financial stability often forced states to bail out credit institutions in distress  in particular systemically important and cross-border  using public funds (bail-outs), which was particularly evident in the great financial crisis after 2008. One could also put it another way: the European legislator  and here you certainly agree with me  first created a very differentiated set of rules for the supervision of credit institutions with the Capital Adequacy Ordinance3 (CRR) and the Capital Requirements Directive IV4 (CRD IV). And immediately afterwards, the same legislator created a set of rules with the BRRD and the Ordinance establishing a Single Bank Resolution Mechanism (SRM)5 in order to allow banks in distress to leave the market as system-friendly as possible. This legislator is therefore aware that even the best possible set of rules for the supervision of credit institutions cannot guarantee that a single bank will not get into difficulties and, if necessary, will be wound up. Banking supervision is therefore not associated with a guarantee of avoidance of insolvency. Insolvencies cannot be prevented, but only their probability of occurrence can be reduced and their negative effects on the banking system as a whole can be reduced. The global "gold standard" of banking supervision, the rules of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, carries exactly this idea  for example in the regulations on loss estimates in the approach based on internal ratings. We can therefore state at this point that banking supervision does not pursue the goal of individual protection (whether supervised or depositor), but of system or collective protection (a functioning banking system as an essential contribution factor to economic prosperity). In addition, there is now a second essential aspect in the specific case. It is not the job of banking supervision to carry out forensic checks and to look for fraud or irregularities in order to prevent or prosecute criminal behaviour. If it were so desired by the legislator, there would be both a legal mandate for supervision and the necessary means and powers in this regard. But that's how we talk about banking supervision, not banking police. Banking supervision is  and this is also clearly evident from the set of standards  in principle designed to supervise reputable actors. This is exactly what the 2 Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD). 3 Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR). 4 Capital Requirements Directive (CRD IV). 5 Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM): Einheitlicher Abwicklungsmechanismus. 2  such as the limited interview possibilities pursuant to  71 (3) BWG, the requirement of undisturbed business operations pursuant to  71 (5) BWG or the limited obligation of the auditor to speak. On the other hand, the public prosecutor's offices are called upon to prosecute criminal behaviour with the investigative powers at their disposal  house searches, communication surveillance, account opening, etc. These facts must be distinguished! The constitutional legislature also distinguishes between these facts and has made powers available to the respective authorities in accordance with them, which ultimately reflect the respective assigned area of responsibility in the severity of their interference with the rights of the individual. It should therefore be noted at this point that the supervisory authority is neither the police nor the public prosecutor's office  and that these areas of responsibility, which are regulated separately by the legislator, should not be mixed with each other as far as possible. Let's get back to the core of banking supervisory activities. Let's stick to my example of equity and take a closer look at the rules that apply to it. Supervisory capital requirements are derived from the risk of a bank's assets. This risk, in turn, reflects the probability of a loss in value of the receivable. In this way, it can be ensured that loss-bearing capital is available with a sufficient confidence interval. However, capital requirements themselves are only one  albeit essential  part of banking regulation. Especially since the financial crisis  keyword Basel III  many further improvements to the regulations and the supervisory system have been introduced. Of course, both the European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS)6 and the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM)7 should be mentioned here. In addition to detailed changes, additional provisions on liquidity requirements (liquidity coverage ratio (LCR)8 and structural liquidity ratio (NSFR)9), leverage ratio10 or systemic risk monitoring by macroprudential supervision have also been introduced, to name a few important improvements. Thanks to these requirements, our banking system has become much more stable, and we are benefiting from this right now. However, I must also honestly mention a trade-off. The banking system is more stable and resilient, but regulation has become more extensive, more detailed and therefore more complex. This is a challenge not only for banks, but also for their auditors. Due to the limited resources, supervisory priorities must be set. In an on-site mission, it is not possible to examine all business areas of a bank taking into account all conceivable risks, but it must be focused specifically on sub-areas evaluated in advance. I would therefore like to invite you to change your perspective and refer to the overwhelming proportion of the activities of Austrian banking supervision, in which, despite the above-mentioned limitations of their task, they are very much involved. 6 European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS): Consisting of the three European Supervisory Authorities (EBA, EIOPA, ESMA) and a Joint Committee ESRB (European Systemic Risk Board). 7 Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM): Single Supervisory Mechanism under the aegis of the ECB. 8 Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): Liquidity coverage ratio to assess short-term liquidity risk. 9 Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR): structural liquidity ratio with a time horizon of one year. 10 Leverage ratio: Leverage ratio based on unweighted equity ratio. 3 does a good job. It is not for nothing that Austrian banking supervision is considered to be very good, as the IMF recently confirmed to us and also leading rating agencies repeatedly emphasize. In the Mattersburg case  as with many other bank insolvencies in the past  official liability is once again being brought into play from several sides. Official liability makes it possible to claim damages from the Federation, the Lander, municipalities and other bodies governed by public law if they have caused damage through unlawful and culpable action within the framework of the sovereign administration. In the past, a very far-reaching application of official liability could be observed in the case of bank insolvencies: In 2003, the Supreme Court still held the view that the instrument of banking supervision is not only intended to counteract the insolvency of banks, but also to protect investors and savers from losses. One can therefore speak here of a very generous interpretation of the protective purpose of the banking supervisory standards. In addition, bank auditors, i.e. the bank's auditors, were also regarded as an auxiliary body of banking supervision and thus assigned to the sovereign enforcement of the Confederation. As a result, the Confederation was liable for the actions of the bank auditors within the framework of the Official Liability Act.11 The Austrian legislature reacted to this case-law in 2005: the Financial Market Supervisory Authority Act expressly excluded the status of bank auditor for the purposes of the Official Liability Act.12 In a further step, in 2008 the official liability of the Confederation for incorrect supervisory behaviour of the Financial Market Authority was restricted. Only damage caused to the supervised legal entities can now be compensated.13 Due to this change in the law, official liability for damages of third parties  i.e. those who are not subject to supervision  is excluded. Of course, this restriction of the protective purpose of banking supervision also includes the Oesterreichische Nationalbank. The OeNB's audit activities are part of the official procedure of the Financial Market Authority. The OeNB does not act independently in this official procedure, but is commissioned by the Financial Market Authority to carry out on-site inspections. The OeNB's role in the FMA's official proceedings corresponds to that of an official expert. The OeNB's actions are therefore attributable to the FMA as the competent supervisory authority.14 Was this legal restriction of the scope of official liability obvious? That question must be answered in the affirmative. According to the German legal situation, which in the past often had a role model effect for the Austrian one, damage to third parties as a result of faulty banking supervision activities has been excluded since 1984.15 The corresponding German Financial Services Supervision Act expressly states that banking supervision is carried out exclusively in the public interest. This simple legal 11 OGH 25.03.2003, 1 Ob 188/02g. 12 Paragraph 3(5) of the FMABG: 'The auditors appointed by the undertakings subject to supervision are not organs within the meaning of Paragraph 1(1) of the AHG, unless they carry out those audits on behalf of the FMA in accordance with the federal laws referred to in Paragraph 2. The same applies to the examination bodies of legally competent examination institutions." 13 Paragraph 3(1)(2) of the FMABG. 14 N. Raschauer, Aktuelle Strukturprobleme des europaischen und osterreichischen Bankenaufsichtsrechts (2010) 404, 407. 15  6 Abs 4 dt KWG aF, now  4 Abs 4 dt FinDAG. 4 Limitation of liability was considered admissible by the German Federal Court of Justice16 in 2005. At the European level, too, the restriction imposed by the German legislator has already occupied the courts.17 In a decision, the ECJ recognised that the Member States were not obliged to establish state liability for incorrect banking supervision in favour of injured depositors. The prerequisite is that the requirements of the Deposit Guarantee Directive are complied with. From a legal point of view, it can therefore be stated that the nature and scope of the statutory exclusion of official liability against depositors made in Germany have been confirmed by both the German and European Supreme Court. Accordingly, such a legal interference with the structure of official liability is also permissible in Austria. There are also plenty of examples of the admissibility of the limitation of official liability in Austria, they sometimes also result from the Official Liability Act itself. Particularly noteworthy here is the absolute limitation period of ten years.18 The limitation of official liability is not only permissible from a legal point of view, it also makes sense from an economic point of view. Naturally, no one who suffers losses actually wants to bear them themselves at the end of the day. This line of thought is now also coming into play in the insolvency of Commerzialbank Mattersburg. However, I would like to return to one of the great lessons of the financial crisis: taxpayers should no longer be liable for bank insolvencies. Together with the improvements in microprudential supervision and the introduction of macroprudential supervision already mentioned above, the BRRD and the Single Resolution Mechanism have created the necessary tools and rules to enable the resolution of banks in distress. The crisis costs caused by the banking system are no longer passed on to the general public, but are in principle to be borne by the owners and creditors. While micro- and macroprudential supervision try to mitigate idiosyncratic or systemic risks as early as possible, a functioning resolution regime should enable the recovery or resolution of a bank in the event of a crisis with the lowest possible costs for the general public. One can think of the whole thing as a network with double bottom: If a bank fails, it should at least be able to exit the market, with the lowest possible costs for the taxpayer, as well as without causing distortions in the financial system. The restriction of the official liability of banking supervision to direct damage to supervised entities introduced by the legislature is therefore consistent with this objective. So it should not come to the situation in which the bail-out of banks, which is complimented by new regulation at the front door, creeps back in through the back door of official liability. This is also necessary in order to avoid years of litigation and uncertainty. 16 BGH 20.01.2005, III ZR 48/01. 17 ECJ 12.10.2004, C-222/02v, ECLI:EU:C:2004:606. 18  6 para 1 sentence 2 AHG. 5 Ultimately, bearing consequences is also an important element for market discipline. If market exits of failing banks are possible, the risk behaviour of relevant stakeholders such as bank management, creditors and investors is not distorted. Capital can therefore be better allocated. However, this credibility and thus the market discipline is endogenous, so it must be created by someone. That is why we in Austria and throughout Europe have complemented this extensive system of banking supervision with macroprudential supervision, bank resolution and deposit insurance. The approach pursued in Austria is a very active one, which tries to link all three areas in order to achieve not only a more stable banking system, but also more sustainable economic growth. One of these areas  deposit insurance  also had to prove its stabilising effect at Commerzialbank Mattersburg. As early as 1983, Diamond/Dybvig showed that "bank runs" cause serious economic problems and can also lead healthy banks into the abyss. The need in the case of bank runs to liquidate assets at adverse prices in the short term also leads to a loss of productivity and a loss of social wealth19. Consequently, it should be noted that the protection of deposits (also) pursues a greater objective than the mere protection of creditors of a bank in distress. It cannot be denied that the establishment of a deposit insurance scheme is accompanied by a certain "moral hazard" in addition to the protection of persons with balances in accounts and savings books. In the currently prevailing system in the EU, deposits of up to EUR 100,000 per customer and bank are secured in one case of security. The logic underlying this restriction, according to which depositors of large amounts are forced to exercise market discipline over the deposit-collecting banks, requires that these depositors are also enabled to exercise that market discipline accordingly by means of adequate transparency of information. For deposits up to an amount of 100,000 euros, a trade off is made between "prevention of bank runs" on the one hand, and "moral hazard" on the other. The fact that such a balancing act must be carried out is probably undeniably necessary and sensible. However, I would like to point out a few other aspects: First of all, if a bank pays excessive interest, for example, and depositors use this, the deposit insurance up to a limit of EUR 100,000 must currently pay for these excessive interest payments in addition to the capital deposited. Here one could certainly think about whether, in addition to the capital, only market interest rates, or, for example, a uniform interest rate, are compensated by the deposit insurance. Of course, it is clear that this is a contribution to the debate which, in view of the associated legislative needs, must also be dealt with at European level in particular. I am also in favour of even greater consideration of a bank's individual risk when assessing its ex-ante contributions to the Deposit Guarantee Fund, within the framework of existing legal possibilities. Again, you can think about whether to use these 19 Diamond/Dybvig, Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance and Liquidity, In: Journal of Political Economy Vol. 91, No. 3 (Jun., 1983), pp. 401-419 6 Possibility should not expand. In this way, the incentive for banks to attract customers with unsustainable interest rates can be reduced. Ultimately, in this context, I consider it essential to improve market transparency and financial literacy. This is the only way to ensure an efficient allocation of capital. To do this, investors must be able to easily access the information necessary to assess the risk. And retail investors need to be aware that a higher return comes with higher risk. Finally, I would like to try to get away from the details and show an adequate solution for the future through an economic view of the big picture. In my opinion, two types of risks have become striking for investors in the present case. First, adverse selection. You choose the wrong company because  for a variety of reasons  you are not able to distinguish a good company from a bad one (also because the latter promises a lot but does not keep it) So you make a decision on the basis of incomplete information that you would not have made if there was complete information. Secondly, the moral hazard that the financial intermediary, aware of the financial security of depositors, is prepared to take on a higher business risk or, in the worst case, even to embezzle funds. Both risks have a common basis, namely information asymmetries  and these are also the starting point for any pyramid scheme, Ponzi scheme or whatever you want to call it. This now seems to have been the case with Commerzialbank Mattersburg as well. Therefore, together with the lessons that can be learned at the legislative level from the Mattersburg, but also Wirecard cases, I also consider it essential to improve market transparency on the one hand, and financial education on the other. Investors need to be able to easily access the information necessary to assess the risk, and every retail investor must also be aware that a higher return goes hand in hand with a higher risk. Ensuring that the individual investor can make an informed decision based on complete information subsequently ensures an efficient allocation of capital. This, ladies and gentlemen, is, in my view, one of the most relevant lessons from the Mattersburg case. Thank you for your attention. I am looking forward to your questions and the discussion. 7

Demzufolge ist festzuhalten, dass die Sicherung von Einlagen (ebenfalls) ein greres Ziel verfolgt als den bloen Schutz von Glubigern einer Bank in Schieflage. Es ist nicht abzustreiten, dass mit der Einrichtung einer Einlagensicherung neben dem Schutz von Personen mit Guthaben auf Konten und Sparbchern auch ein gewisser moral hazard einhergeht. Im derzeit in der EU vorherrschenden System werden in einem Sicherungsfall Einlagen bis zu 100.000 EUR pro Kunde und Bank abgesichert. Die dieser Beschrnkung zugrundeliegende Logik, wonach Einleger grerer Betrge gezwungen sind die Marktdisziplin ber die einlagensammelnden Banken auszuben, bedingt, dass diese Einleger durch eine entsprechend adquate Informationstransparenz auch in die Lage versetzt werden, diese Marktdisziplin entsprechend ausben zu knnen. Bei Einlagen bis zu einem Betrag von 100.000 Euro wird also ein trade off zwischen Verhinderung von Bank Runs auf der einen, und moral hazard auf der anderen Seite vorgenommen. Dass eine solche Abwgung vorzunehmen ist, ist wohl unbestreitbar notwendig und sinnvoll. Ich mchte aber noch auf einige Aspekte hinweisen: Zunchst, wenn eine Bank etwa berhhte Zinsen bezahlt, und Einleger dies nutzen, muss derzeit die Einlagensicherung bis zu einer Grenze von 100.000 EUR neben dem eingelegten Kapital auch fr diese berhhten Zinszahlungen aufkommen. Hier knnte man sicherlich darber nachdenken, ob neben dem Kapital nur marktbliche Zinsen, oder beispielsweise ein einheitlicher Zinssatz, von der Einlagensicherung abgegolten werden. Wobei selbstverstndlich klar ist, dass es sich hier um einen Diskussionsbeitrag handelt, der  angesichts der damit einhergehenden Notwendigkeiten in der Rechtsetzung - insbesondere auch auf europischer Ebene zu behandeln ist. Zudem befrworte ich eine noch strkere Bercksichtigung des individuellen Risikos einer Bank bei der Bemessung ihrer ex-ante Beitrge zum Einlagensicherungsfonds im Rahmen der bereits bestehenden rechtlichen Mglichkeiten. Auch hier kann man darber nachdenken, ob man diese 19 Diamond/Dybvig, Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance and Liquidity, In: Journal of Political Economy Vol. 91, No. 3 (Jun., 1983), pp. 401-419 6 Mglichkeit nicht erweitern sollte. So kann der Anreiz fr Banken, Kunden mit nicht nachhaltigen Zinsen zu locken, verringert werden. Letztlich halte ich in diesem Zusammenhang eine Verbesserung der Marktransparenz und der Finanzbildung fr essenziell. Nur so kann eine effiziente Allokation von Kapital sichergestellt werden. Dazu mssen Investoren leicht an die zur Einschtzung des Risikos notwendigen Informationen gelangen knnen. Und Kleinanleger mssen sich bewusst sein, dass eine hhere Rendite mit einem hheren Risiko einhergeht. Zum Abschluss mchte ich versuchen, von den Details wegzukommen und durch einen konomischen Blick auf das groe Ganze einen adquate Lsungsansatz fr die Zukunft aufzeigen. Meiner Meinung nach sind zwei Arten von Risiken fr Anleger im gegenstndlichen Fall schlagend geworden. Erstens: adverse Selektion. Man entscheidet sich fr das falsche Unternehmen, da man  aus vielfltigen Grnden - gar nicht in der Lage ist, ein gutes Unternehmen von einem Schlechten zu unterscheiden (auch weil letzteres vieles verspricht aber nicht hlt) Man trifft also eine Entscheidung auf Basis unvollstndiger Informationen, die man bei vollstndiger Informationslage so gar nicht getroffen htte. Zweitens: der moralische Hazard, dass der Finanzintermedir wissend um die finanzielle Absicherung der Einleger bereit ist, ein hheres Geschftsrisiko einzugehen oder im schlimmsten Fall gar Gelder veruntreut werden. Beide Risiken haben eine gemeinsame Grundlage, nmlich Informationsasymmetrien  und diese sind auch der Ausgangspunkt fr jedes Pyramidenspiel, Schneeballsystem, Ponzi-Scheme oder wie immer sie es nennen wollen. Das scheint nun auch bei der Commerzialbank Mattersburg so gewesen zu sein. Daher halte ich  zusammen mit den Lehren, die man auf gesetzgebender Ebene aus den Fllen Mattersburg, aber auch Wirecard ziehen kann - auch eine Verbesserung der Marktransparenz auf der einen Seite, und der Finanzbildung auf der anderen Seite fr essenziell. Investoren mssen leicht an die zur Einschtzung des Risikos notwendigen Informationen gelangen knnen, und auch jedem Kleinanleger muss bewusst sein, dass eine hhere Rendite mit einem hheren Risiko einhergeht. Wenn sichergestellt wird, dass der einzelne Anleger auf Basis vollstndiger Informationen eine informierte Entscheidung treffen kann, sorgt dies in weiterer Folge fr eine effiziente Allokation von Kapital. Dies, geschtzte Damen und Herren, ist meines Erachtens eine der relevantesten Lehren aus dem Fall Mattersburg. Vielen Dank fr Ihre Aufmerksamkeit. Ich freue mich schon auf Ihre Fragen und die Diskussion. 7

Title: Speech at the first constituent meeting of the Austrian Payments Board
text: Univ.-Prof. Mag. Dr. Robert Holzmann Governor Oesterreichische Nationalbank NETWORK Vienna, 27 January 2021 Speech by Governor Holzmann at the first constituent meeting of the Austrian Payments Board on 27.01.2021 As Governor of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB), I would like to extend a very warm welcome to the inaugural meeting of the Austrian Payments Board (APB). Due to COVID-19 measures, this session is now held exclusively virtually. I particularly welcome the participating bank boards of all domestic banking groups or sectors and the Managing Director of the Federal Division of Banking and Insurance of the WKO. I also welcome my colleagues on the OeNB's Board of Directors, the OeNB's representatives of payment transactions and the management of OeNPAY Financial Innovation HUB-GmbH. Today's meeting will be moderated by Dr. Augustin, OeNB Director of the Investments, Payments and Internal Services Department. On this occasion, I would also like to thank Mrs Mag. Petia Niederlander, who will succeed Dr. Augustin this year as a result of his retirement in the area of payment transactions and is already making her debut today in the sense of a well-coordinated handover. With the closing of the "Felix Austria" project at the end of 2020, a major and important milestone for the restructuring of the set-up of Austrian retail payment transactions was very successfully completed. The transition of "system ownership" to the "clearing service" went smoothly at the beginning of the year thanks to the participation of all project participants as well as your houses. A heartfelt thank you here at this point to all those who have contributed to this success. Thus, important steps for the necessary structural adjustment of the operational set-up of Austrian retail payment transactions, as envisaged from the outset by the "Felix Austria" project, have now been successfully completed and a clear future distribution of tasks and roles has been implemented. Due to numerous lessons learned in recent years, including in the "Felix Austria" project, and the current major and rapid changes in the environment, a great need for coordination and action was recognized for the best possible, structured further development of the domestic financial centre, in particular the future topic of payment transactions. Consequently, the Executive Board of the OeNB decided to set up a coordination platform at Executive Board level for the Austrian financial centre as a central bank, which meets at least annually, Publisher and editor: Oesterreichische Nationalbank Press Office Vienna 9., Otto-Wagner-Platz 3 P.O. Box 61, 1010 Vienna the so-called "Austrian Payments Board (APB)". The objective of the "Austrian Payments Board" is to contribute to the efficient and rapid further development of Austrian market infrastructures and projects relevant to payment transactions for the benefit of all "stakeholders" of the Austrian financial centre by coordinating joint projects and initiatives. Furthermore, the Board also serves the exchange of information and the coordination of common Austrian positions of all relevant "stakeholders" in payment transactions for the European and international level. Why is coordination and joint action in retail payment transactions so important from the OeNB's point of view right now? 1. Digitalization Non-cash payment transactions cover more and more areas and areas of application of our daily lives and thus acquire an increasingly important economic importance as a critical digital infrastructure of Austria as the "bloodstream" of our economy. The COVID-19 pandemic is now proving to be an additional trend accelerator and thus a "game changer", also in terms of changes in payment behaviour or, for example, the importance of online trading. 2. European competitiveness In the increasingly lucrative payments market, Austrian and European banks as traditional payment service providers are increasingly competing with international "BigTechs", mainly from Asia and the USA, at the customer interface. The topics of data protection and data sovereignty as well as the preservation of value creation power are also becoming increasingly important in this context from a pan-European perspective. Away from niches, institutional, regional, but also national lone fighters against these very powerful global challenges currently seem unpromising. Austrian technology companies and start-ups that take into account the interests of retailers and banks should  where possible  also have equal competitive opportunities. The support of and neutrality for local and app/smartphone-based payment providers vis-a-vis international competitors should in any case be made possible at European level. 3. European solutions At the European level, too, various solutions are currently being sought in the light of the challenges presented. The European Commission and the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Eurosystem have clearly recognised that in order to strengthen the financial and economic sovereignty of the EU and the international role of the euro, the monetary union and the euro as a common currency must also be completed in the non-cash area through further measures and initiatives. This includes, in particular, the strengthening of competitiveness, independence and (operational) security in European retail payments, which are also important common challenges for the political levels and institutions of Europe. However, strategic autonomy in the digital sphere, not only vis-a-vis China, but above all also vis-a-vis the US "BigTechs", is not very credible as long as there is no common "federal" digital architecture. To date, EU digital policy is certainly not sufficiently holistic. A development from 2 systemic, non-technological point of view is required, a regulatory approach alone is not enough. As the OeNB, we will continue to be committed to the national interest at various levels in order to promote pan-European payment solutions and also to ensure compatibility and interoperability with our national systems and end-user requirements. Private-sector pan-European initiatives are also of great importance here and require our cooperation. Mrs. Mag. Dutch will give us a corresponding update on the current status of the European Payments Initiative (EPI) today. It is important to ensure the harmonisation of the rules, infrastructures and supervision within which the various pan-European solutions operate. In general, technical innovations such as instant payments/TIPS are to be regarded as a basic requirement, but from an economic point of view as mandatory prerequisites for participation ("qualifiers") for banks in future competition with alternative providers of payment services. The timely roll-out of Instant Payments and the further bundling of the innovative strength of the Austrian financial centre therefore seem to make sense for maintaining competitiveness and as a location security for Austria and its digital infrastructure. Ensuring efficient, secure and future-proof retail payment transactions for Austria is therefore an essential strategic objective for the OeNB from a locational and economic point of view. In agreement with the European Commission and the ECB, we at the OeNB regard the prompt nationwide provision of all Austrians with interoperable, account-based real-time payment options in euros (instant payments) in the SEPA area as a quasi "New Normal". As part of the "Felix Austria" project, PSA and its owner banks have announced that they will set up a new, instant-capable retail payment system for Austria in the next few years (expected in 2023) and offer instant payment payments for all domestic banks on the same terms as traditional transfers. However, this now also requires a rapid roll-out of instant payment initiatives in Austria in order not to fall behind or be substituted compared to other forms of payment. For this rapid roll-out, the integration of stationary and online retail will play an important role. Let us therefore maintain the momentum from the "Felix Austria" project and discuss or then take the necessary first steps for 2021 and beyond today to make this vision a reality. On the part of the OeNB, we propose the following steps for the fastest possible dissemination of offers for real-time payments in euros for Austria: Step 1: Accelerate instant payment accessibility ( interoperability) Step 2: Integration into core banking systems Step 3: Link with additional functions for customer benefit These steps require a national solidarity of all key stakeholders in Austria analogous to successful large-scale projects of the past as well as the best possible coordination of the various committees and an exchange of knowledge on European and international 3 Plain. As usual, the OeNB will act as a neutral intermediary so that Austrian banks can continue to be successful at the customer interface in the face of increasingly international competition in the future and make their contribution to the well-being of Austria. As of today, the Austrian Payments Board as well as the projects and initiatives of OeNPAY are available to us for this purpose. I look forward to your active participation and hand over the floor to Dr. Augustin as moderator. 4
